quest.title: Gradus ad Capitolium
quest.description: After passing through the perilous oceanic trench, you finally arrive at the ancient sunken capital of Remuria. Next, you must head to "Domus Aurea" for a showdown with Boethius...
quest.rewards_formatted: Adventure EXP x300, Primogem x40, Mora x30000, Hero's Wit x2, Mystic Enhancement Ore x3

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: Phew! We're finally here!

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: And there's Domus Aurea. It looks more like a giant harp, though. Why did your Sebastos construct it like that?

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Yeah, nothing like the rest of the stuff we saw up there.

response.speaker: Monsieur Os
response.text: Of course. This palace was fashioned from a giant ship. It was designed to be a titanic instrument on which the symphony was to be played.

response.speaker: Monsieur Os
response.text: See those pipes extending outward? Though the symphony now lies broken, this was once how it would be broadcast to the four corners of the world.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: The whole palace is an instrument!? The entire thing!?

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Uhh, then, wouldn't this entire water body start vibrating if it were to play? We might get blasted apart like tofu if we get too close...

response.speaker: Monsieur Os
response.text: Meow, meow? What is tofu?

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Wait, you've never had any, Osse? Uh, then it might be hard to explain. We could always take you to go have some next time... Wait, can cats even eat tofu?

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: The "Eternal City," indeed... Remus's will protects this place still, just as I expected. No wonder that brazen, shameless traitor has endured even til this day...

response.speaker: Monsieur Os
response.text: Hmph. I imagine that Boethius owes his survival of time's erosion to having laid low in the palace for all these millennia.

response.speaker: Monsieur Os
response.text: And over those long years, he gradually mastered the power of Phobos...

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Well, now that we're here, we should meet up with that rude guy. He might just be shocked to see us for all you know!

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: In that case, let us part ways for now.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Huh? You're not coming along?

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Hah. Why would you think that? I merely do not wish to see that particular one again.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: I wish to never again hear a word from that devil's mouth. His words are a sham, and shameful are his lies. See that you do not fall for them!

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Besides, I could not help you even if I came with you, for I am but a temporary occupant of this Ichor-made body.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Were battle to be joined, I would have no recourse...

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Not that I would mind terribly, but no gain would salve the loss of his seizing the symphony that Remus bequeathed unto me.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Let us part here for now. Though I cannot aid you in battle, I can use the currents to send you hence. Come to me, should you need such aid.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Regardless, let us meet again once you have vanquished that traitor.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: When that time comes, perhaps I too shall have the chance to make amends for my past regrets.

choices.text: You've been a great help already.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Haha, and I was pleased to be of aid! But to tell the truth, I have no desire to see that one ever again.

choices.text: Completely different from all the ruins above.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Yeah, it feels like this only just sunk.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Cassiodor, dear friend! I knew you would come.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Ah, and the uninvited barbarians...

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: When it comes down to it, you're not the boss of this place. Besides, it was Osse who brought us here — that counts as an invitation as far as Paimon's concerned!

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: Really, you're the discourteous one here.

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: Exactly! And we've heard all about it, you know! All the bad stuff you've done...

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Silence, you noisome, obstreperous insects... I am speaking to Cassiodor. Do not interrupt!

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: #{NICKNAME}, Paimon, I'll take care of this.

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: Boethius, I have come as promised. Honor your pledge, and relinquish the souls of the surface dwellers.

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: They do not deserve to suffer this unforeseen calamity... The grudges between us should stay between us.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: You... call this "unforeseen"!?

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Have you not looked upon our kindred? They lie trapped in these lightless waters, like walking corpses!

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Are they not supposed to walk upon sunlit shores?

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: If my brief internment of surface-folk souls is a disaster bereft of rhyme and reason, then what would you call the millennia-long suffering of our kind?

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Listen, and listen well! The judgment of the surface peoples has only just begun!

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: No. The one who imprisoned them was you. And it was you who turned our kin into monsters.

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: They... We once had a choice. So long as we discarded our old grudges, the Mistress of Waters agreed to accept us into a new nation.

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: But you used them, took advantage of their pain, their trust in you. You turned them into tools of your ambition.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: That was their choice. They chose the old order, not the honeyed death you brought.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: And just as they gave unto us the conducting batons the Sebastos bestowed upon them, so too are we duty-bound to lead them unto the correct path.

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: How dare you swagger, you shameless traitor! You who betrayed the Sebastos's trust, and led our nation to ruin!

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Hah! I hear that vile dragon's slander in your words. And you would believe a foe of our nation, rather than your kin and comrades!?

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: I serve no god, no king. Only mighty Remuria, and our noble ideals.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Remus proved unworthy to reign supreme from the moment he uttered that perverse command. And so, there are no traitors. If anything, it was I who rescued our nation from his error.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: He colluded with our foes, commanding the vile drake to flatten our cities. He even attempted to destroy the Grand Symphony, which would have consigned us to live under Fortuna's yoke once more.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: How could I have stood aside and done nothing in the face of his madness?

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: And so you betrayed him. You shut the Initium Iani... and in the end, Phobos's power went out of control, and the royal palace sank into the depths...

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Will you not open your eyes to the truth? It was Remus who betrayed us, betrayed Phobos. That was the true prelude to tragedy.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: I have already spent thousands of years struggling to recreate the symphony of the past, weaving the broken melodies together in the deep waters just to recreate what you hear now.

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: No... In your hands, it has become harsh, and the discordant voices of agony and hate denounce your violence.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Hah, and who decides what is harmonious or not? Is it not absolute power? Remus bent the knee to the savages and odious dragons precisely because he failed to comprehend this.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: But it matters not. This inverted world shall soon be righted, and I shall become the new Sebastos!

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: That is impossible, Boethius. You are but a mortal human! Humans can never become gods...

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: But ah, Cassiodor, you forget! Was Remus's ideal not for all humans to become gods? To seize their own destinies?

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Do you not remember? Did the rites we researched and recorded in the golden castellum not chart a course to that very destination?

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: But we did not then know what lay beyond. Had we known, those thousands of years ago, we...

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Times have changed! Things are different now, Cassiodor. Join us. My preparations are complete. Only together can we accomplish this deed.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: I have rid my soul of all impurities, obtaining a true will. The stairway to heaven is but a single step away!

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: I merely need to gather all wills that have been scattered throughout the waters — yes, even yours, which Remus personally severed.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Two minds shall merge into one, and thus shall Remuria be whole once more — once more clad in immortal form, infused with refined steel and stone.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: I... No, we, shall "take on flesh" once more, and a new Sebastos shall be born... But not only that! I shall also gain that which even Remus could not attain — the power to change the very essence of this world.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: I will turn back the wheel of fate, usher in the old world's return, and bring justice to the land. The surface dwellers shall submit to our will, as they must.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: It shall be as the hymn says: "And when they use their will to command, the rest shall bow down and listen."

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: You know I will not acknowledge you. You have defiled his ideals.

dialogues.speaker: Monsieur Os
dialogues.text: I will uphold my own justice.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Hmph! It matters not! You will understand once you enter Phobos's melody — then, you shall join me!

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Since you insist on sabotaging my plans, I'm afraid I'll have to ask you to stay in my palace for a while longer.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: I cannot detain you for long, of course, but it should be long enough. Let us meet again when I become a god and sit upon the Sebastos's throne.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Before that, let my little ensemble occupy you for a time.
#{NICKNAME}! I've found you at last...

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: Cassiodor, you mean! I believe you might have met me in the Sebastos's memories, though I suppose this is our first time meeting in this manner.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: Time is short. Maintaining this form in Boethius's symphonic palace is no easy task.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: Let us keep this brief.

response.speaker: Player
response.text: Where are we, exactly?

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: This is a space created by Boethius, the manifestation of his soul.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: It is maintained, just as the Sebastos's memories you entered before are, by the grace of the symphony's might.

response.speaker: Player
response.text: So just now...

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: Yes. He used the music's power to pull us in.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: I suspect that Domus Aurea is too close to the heart of the Phobos, allowing him to directly influence the present world.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: If we truly allow him to obtain power that surpasses reality, he might even pull the entire surface world into this space.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: When that happens, his delusions will replace the real world, and Fontaine will revert to its appearance from thousands of years ago.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: Just like what happened in Petrichor... No, I suspect it would be worse still.

response.speaker: Player
response.text: Will he really become a god?

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: That depends on your definition. It is not hard to give shape to false fantasies, but he will find transcending fate futile.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: Were it truly that simple, then those thousands of years ago... we would have already succeeded.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: All he can do now is drag more innocents into the nightmare of his making, turning them into walking, corpse-like puppets.

response.speaker: Player
response.text: Then we must stop him.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: That we do, but that cannot be done here. You must return to the real world.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: In that, I shall aid you.

response.speaker: Player
response.text: And what about you?

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: Not to worry. He has no plans for me at the moment. As for me, I've just thought of a way in which we can destroy him utterly.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: He has prepared a mighty form for himself in the real world, and plans to initiate a ritual within Domus Aurea that will have him "take on flesh."

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: As long as we can get him to lower his guard and gather the symphony scattered throughout the deep waters into that body...

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: We can seize that opportunity to destroy both him and that body. That will put an end to everything.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: #Only you can do this, {NICKNAME}.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: Phobos's melody does not sing of your destiny, and Boethius cannot influence your soul.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: You are the exception to all that is planned. Perhaps that is why the Sebastos guided you here...

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: Go now. My strength will not hold for long.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: Let us meet again in the real world, and we may yet bring an end to this long nightmare.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: Indeed, it is I! I believe you might have met me in the Sebastos's memories, though I suppose this is our first time meeting in this manner.

response.speaker: Cassiodor
response.text: Haha, well, you might have seen me in the Sebastos's memories, but I believe this is our first meeting in this manner.

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: Aaaah! You finally woke up!

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: Paimon was worried sick! She thought... she thought you might have had your soul stolen by that jerk, just like all the townspeople!

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: *sniff* You'd better be!

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: After you passed out, Boethius and Monsieur Os disappeared along with that wave of sound, leaving Paimon all alone here...

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: And then this big guy came along. Not that he helped much either...

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: I fear that was not up to me. I am but a soul that dwells within the Ichor, and though that Remus did give me his final symphony...

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: But to wield its power against Boethius is a different matter.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: #Anyway, {NICKNAME}'s woken up and seems okay at least, but where'd Monsieur Os go? Did Boethius...

response.speaker: Player
response.text: I saw him.

response.speaker: Black Screen
response.text: You tell of what happened within Boethius's soul-palace.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Huh? So Monsieur Os is in there alone?

choices.text: He seems to have his own plan. Don't worry.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Regardless, should he prove correct, then we still have a chance to defeat that shameless devil. But first, you must enter Domus Aurea...

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Well then, big guy...

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: What are you looking at me for?

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Didn't you once lead a host of dragons to attack Remuria's capital? Getting us into Domus Aurea should be a piece of cake!

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: You have many ideas for one so small, little one. Still, this shall not prove as simple as you think.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: The chief strength of Dragonborn lies in our powerful flesh. Embedded into Ichor as I am, all that remains to me is but the feeblest of wills.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Destroying the Initium Iani exhausted nigh all my power — and Domus Aurea, defended by the symphony's power, cannot be compared to gates of mere stone.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Wait, then aren't we fresh outta options? Are we really just gonna watch while that Boethius guy eats Monsieur Os up!?

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Peace, you rash little thing. I merely said that I was powerless, but it is not so for you.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: The power of the symphony defends the palace. That same strength can be used to break it.

response.speaker: Player
response.text: But the symphony that I can wield is...

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Yeah! That super-powerful Phobos thing is protecting the palace, right? How can we possibly beat it...

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: If you cannot beat it, then simply borrow what you need from it!

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Once upon a time, the will of Phobos flowed through golden aqueducts into every corner of Remuria.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Though these paths and pipes have been destroyed, if you can connect the section that lies before you once more...

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: The great gates of Domus Aurea shall surely open, just as they once did. That is what is written in the symphony, after all!

choices.text: Sounds like it's worth a shot.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: I too made some discoveries while searching for anything Remus might have left behind. It appears that this devil has yet to join some fragments of the symphony to his music, and they are scattered in this part of the sea.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Come with me. If we can find them and use their strength, we might yet reverse the flow of time and return the aqueducts to their original form.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Ooh, that does sound kinda promising! Let's get a move on, then!

choices.text: Looks like we don't have other options...

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: That's right, and after that, Boethius and Monsieur Os disappeared along with that wave of sound, leaving Paimon all alone here...

talks.objective: Head to where the golden aqueducts are

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: Alrighty, looks like the waterways are reconnected!

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: Next, we should go back and look for that big lunk, eh?

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: Hmm... Paimon wonders how Monsieur Os is doing. We've gotta hurry up!

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: #Huh? {NICKNAME}? What's going on? Is it happening again...?

talks.objective: Head to where the golden aqueducts are

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: Remus, I must remind you...

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: That in my view, both your kingdom and the symphony you composed are now beyond your control.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: Though I have never expected much from those created by the Usurper of the Many Waters and nurtured by yourself, the extent of their degradation is shocking nonetheless.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: The civilization created by you and your subjects shone brighter than all others in this world, but naught remains now but deep, impenetrable darkness.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: The atrocities committed in the name of civilization and order were far crueler than even pure barbarism. Even the most savage and violent of vishaps would never engage in such meaningless slaughter.

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: I am perfectly aware of all that you say...

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: You know, and yet you remain indifferent? Or are you powerless?

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: No. You could easily destroy those mortals who deserve punishment if you so wished, but you cannot bring yourself to do it.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: You love humanity. This is the curse you bear as a usurper.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: It is time for me to depart... I will not aid them in butchering innocent mortals, but neither do I harbor any desire to stop them.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: You once promised the Usurper of Many Waters that you would use the pure water she granted you to create a world of endless prosperity, one without conflict.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: I followed you to the surface precisely because I wished to witness that future, but this is how it turned out... You have failed, Remus. You could not defeat "fa{RUBY#[D]Fortuna}te."

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: Blood shall stain the High Sea red once more — such is the cruelty the heavens show to their creations.

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: I have a plan...

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: Oh? You always were one to have many plans, Remus. But all of them lie in the dust now. Even you do not know where it all went wrong.

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: Would you like to hear it, though? This will be the last one.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: I distinctly recall you saying the same thing when you persuaded me to leave the Fontemer... But speak now, before I return there, to the side of the Usurper of Many Waters.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: Hahaha! Fascinating. Fascinating!

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: Only you could be so toweringly selfish, yet so utterly selfless!

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: You even took me into account, did you? Recklessness. How terribly rash of you, usurper-lord of mortals.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: Still, your plot pleases me.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: The mere thought of leading my vishaps and trampling your arrogant, foolish people underfoot brings me joy.

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: But this shall be mere ceremony. Just a show...

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: Fret not. I shall be as you said — merciful.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: But if you do this, your life as a god shall come to an end. There will be nothing left but the symphony. Have you considered this fully?

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: Of course. Of course.

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: The box of horrors that I opened, so too shall I shut.

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: Good. Then I accept your proposal. If the time should come, I shall join my strength to that of your symphony...

dialogues.speaker: Scylla
dialogues.text: Phobos's chains shall be broken, and your people shall once more be free.

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: In that case, please accept...

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: My final... symphony.

talks.objective: Head to where the golden aqueducts are

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: #Did you see Remus's memories again, {NICKNAME}?

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: It wasn't another one of Mr. Evil-and-Rude's this time, right?

dialogues.speaker: Paimon
dialogues.text: Even in dreams, that jerk's just super irritating!

choices.text: I think I know what Remus's plan was...

response.speaker: Player
response.text: To accomplish it, we will need to play Scylla's symphony.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Eh? What's with that all of a sudden? What did you see in the memory?

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Fascinating. Remus's power lingers still in the deep seas, and has not dispersed... and I, too, am here at last. Do you know what that means?

response.speaker: Player
response.text: The conditions have been fulfilled.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Indeed. That is why I have come here with you. To make amends for millennia of regret.

response.speaker: Player
response.text: Now, the final question is Phobos...

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: Wait, wait! Paimon's confused! What are we using the music for? It's nice that you understand each other and all... But you're leaving Paimon out!

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: That's unfair! Tell her what's going on!

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: The final symphony Remus gave me, or the Requiem, is an order for the Phobos to self-destruct.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: He was to sacrifice himself to unleash the symphony's power, and it would fall to me to control the primordial, savage energies that he would awaken.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: That was how he would free his subjects from their stone bodies and give them back forms of flesh and blood, destroying the artificial barrier between races.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: He once instructed me not to reveal this plan to any of his subjects, for it was only by making them realize their limitations that prejudice and arrogance could be set aside.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: #It appears, however, that you have pieced together his plan through the memories he left behind, {NICKNAME}.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: So that's what happened... But his sacrifice was wasted in the end...

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Perhaps, but now that my soul has been freed, there is a chance to make amends.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: The lost souls of Remus's former subjects remain imprisoned in their statues. If we defeat that monstrosity...

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: We can use the Requiem to give their souls release, allowing them to return to the High Sea, to the eternal cycle of life and death.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: That way, I may consider myself to have fulfilled his wish.

response.speaker: Player
response.text: Perhaps that is why I came here.

response.speaker: Scylla
response.text: Indeed, outlander. Perhaps this is indeed a fated encounter.

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: (This is... Domus Aurea.)

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: (Have I entered Remus's memory again?)

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: (No, the atmosphere... it's different from before.)

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Welcome to my palace, outlander. My symphony.

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: Boethius!?

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Do not be startled. Have we not met aforetime, and more than once?

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Whether through my phantom in the real world, or in the memory-palaces Remus left behind.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: But this is no phantasm of Remus's memory. This is my symphony. My golden stage.

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: I knew it...

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: Wails of sorrow ring off every wall...

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Is that so, outlander? I know not from whence you came...

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: It seems you are not a human birthed from the primordial waters, nor are you any surface being at all.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: I cannot see the color of your soul, nor can I touch it.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Nonetheless, this is not your war. My vengeance against the surface dwellers is none of your concern.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: I know not why you hinder our work.

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: For Monsieur Os...

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Ah, but can your short friendship surpass the span of our kinship?

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Cassiodor and I... We were new hu{RUBY#[D]golems}mans crafted by Remus's own hand, and we are the final survivors.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Compared with our other kin, his soul is like insoluble Ichor.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Other than myself, only he has true will, and only when we are combined, can we become a complete "self."

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: "So too are our wills one." The opera's final act shall see him return to us. This is his "fate."

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: To save the people of Petrichor...

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Those people... They are neither your kin nor your subjects.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: On the contrary, so far are you above them that they may as well be ants. Perhaps not even that.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: The weak should submit to the strong. Is that not the law that this world should follow?

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: And yet, you say you will protect them? Is this your boundless mercy? Or simply folly?

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: For the justice in this world...

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Justice? You can't actually be serious, can you?

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: You may possess power that even I cannot perceive, but you would be naive, outlander, to think that brute force alone will defeat me.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: I have long become one with the symphony that fills these deep seas. Even if you should destroy my physical form, so long as the agonized waters flow, and so long as the memories of vengeance do not fade...

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: My will shall not perish, and I shall remain a nightmare that haunts this world.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Unless you choose as Cassiodor... as that stray cat did, exiling oneself to become the jailer of the old world... But I do not believe that one so distinguished as you would do so.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Forsake that superfluous sympathy of yours! Should the guilty not be punished? Is that not justice?

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: Guilty, you say... They are innocent.

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: No Fontainian is innocent! They are the spawn of our barbarian foes...

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Their ancestors seized from us the realms that should have been ours by right, and they must pay the price for that original sin!

dialogues.speaker: Boethius
dialogues.text: Have you anything else to say, outlander?
